html:
The Makah are an Indigenous people of Cape Flattery, the northwestern tip of Washington State, where the Strait of Juan de Fuca meets the Pacific. Their language is Wakashan, close to that of the Nuu-chah-nulth across the strait on Vancouver Island, not Salish like that of the Coast Salish to the east.

They were whalers, going out in cedar canoes to hunt grey and humpback whales, and they also fished halibut and salmon and hunted seals. At the village of Ozette a mudslide in the 1700s buried several houses. Dug out from 1970, the Ozette site gave thousands of wooden tools, baskets and carvings, preserved by the wet clay.

In the Treaty of Neah Bay of 1855 they gave up most of their land but kept the right to hunt whales. They revived the hunt in 1999, which drew both support and protest.
